# Standardized values

The units rule for standard deviation and the notation in
\longref{notation-sigma-s} help us interpret a standardized value. The
definition in \longref{defn-sample-standard-deviation} supplies the measure of
spread. The warning about the 68% rule limits what we can infer from the
standard deviation.

:::: {.Definition #defn-z-score}
## Standardized value

A **standardized value**, or **z-score**, measures how far an observation sits
from the mean in standard-deviation units. Positive values sit above the mean,
and negative values sit below it.

::: {#formula-z-score .details .formula-details summary="Details and formulas"
non-interactive-summary="Formula"}

For an observation $x$, mean $\bar{x}$, and sample standard deviation $s$,

$$
z = \frac{x-\bar{x}}{s}.
$$

Subtracting the mean measures the observation's distance from the center.
Dividing by the standard deviation expresses that distance in units of
ordinary variation.

:::
::::

::: {.callout-note}
## Key idea: Comparable scales

Standardizing removes the original measurement units. We can therefore compare
relative positions for variables measured on different scales.
:::

:::: {.Exercise #exercise-z-score}
## Delivery-time z-score

A delivery took 20 minutes in a sample with mean 14 minutes and standard
deviation 3 minutes. What is its z-score?

::: {#solution-z-score .details .solution-details summary="Solution" display="show"
non-interactive-summary="Solution"}

The delivery is 6 minutes above the mean. Dividing that distance by the
3-minute standard deviation gives $z=2$, so the delivery sits two standard
deviations above the mean.

:::
::::

::: {.TechnicalDetail #technical-long-page-break}
## Sampling variability and the $n-1$ correction

The sample mean comes from the same observations whose spread we want to
measure. It follows the observations toward whichever values happened to enter
the sample. That movement makes the observations look a little closer to their
sample mean than they are to the population mean.

Suppose repeated samples come from the same population. A sample containing
several unusually high observations will usually have an unusually high sample
mean. Those observations are far from the population mean, but the shifted
sample mean moves toward them and shortens their measured deviations.

The same pattern holds for an unusually low sample. Its sample mean shifts
downward, again reducing the deviations measured inside that sample. Dividing
the sum of squared deviations by $n$ preserves this systematic
understatement.

The $n-1$ denominator compensates for the mean's movement. Under independent
sampling from a population with finite variance, the resulting sample variance
has the correct population variance as its average across repeated samples.
This is a statement about repeated sampling, not a promise about one dataset.

The degrees-of-freedom explanation describes the same correction from another
direction. The deviations from the sample mean add to zero. If a sample has
five observations and we know four deviations, the fifth must balance the
other four.

Only four deviations can vary freely in that example. More generally, fitting
the sample mean uses one degree of freedom and leaves $n-1$ for estimating
spread. The correction matters most in small samples because $n$ and $n-1$
become nearly identical as the sample size grows.

This correction makes the sample variance unbiased for the population
variance. Taking the square root does not preserve that exact unbiasedness, so
the sample standard deviation can still be slightly low on average. In most
introductory applications, using $n-1$ remains the standard calculation.
:::
